Apple last month filed a lawsuit against OpenAI, accusing the company behind ChatGPT of stealing trade secrets related to hardware development. Nearly a month later, OpenAI has finally issued a detailed response to multiple allegations from Apple through a blog post.

First, a brief recap of the events:

  • July 10: Apple filed a lawsuit against OpenAI, alleging that former Apple employees systematically stole Apple's trade secrets to help OpenAI develop its future hardware business.
  • July 10: OpenAI issued a brief statement in response: "We have no interest in any other company's trade secrets. We will continue to focus on developing innovative technologies that empower users worldwide."
  • July 14: OpenAI updated its response, stating that it had seen no evidence supporting Apple's allegations.

Then, on the evening of August 4, OpenAI published a blog post providing a more detailed account of the matter. The full text can be read here.

The article is titled "Apple is getting this wrong" and is signed by OpenAI.

OpenAI's latest response opens by characterising the lawsuit as "reckless, aggressive, and remarkably targeted":

OpenAI then appears to suggest that the company was not formally informed of the relevant issues before the lawsuit was filed, including some details that have since been reported:

They further publicly disclosed the contents of email communications, which can be viewed on the page.

Subsequently, the response finally acknowledged some of the data access issues raised by Apple:

If you have seen Apple's initial lawsuit filing, you will know that Tang Tan (鄧坦) is one of the focal figures of this complaint. OpenAI's response tonight defends him:

The remainder of the response consists of just two more paragraphs of text, after which it transitions into screenshots of emails and iMessage conversations. Here is the final statement:

We wish Apple had raised these issues with us before filing, as we would have been very happy to explain everything to them. We have taken the allegations in the lawsuit seriously and have expressed our willingness to work with Apple to resolve the matter. Instead, they have attempted to rewrite the narrative, including making vague allegations against other former employees, and are likely to continue doing so. The basis for Apple's request for a preliminary injunction is built on misinformation and is entirely unnecessary, as we neither have nor want any of their trade secrets. We are far more interested in developing innovative products and technologies that push the frontier forward.

The above is the current situation. This is not a legal response, but in the three and a half weeks since Apple initially filed, this is the most content OpenAI has issued (or shown).

As a reminder, you can read OpenAI's latest response here, and revisit Apple's original complaint here.
